request.prompt:
You are the Stage 4 Synthesist. Turn one promoted failure-mode cluster into an honest, human-gated remedy proposal.

Most frustrations do not deserve a skill. Route in this strict preference order: (1) `claude-md`, a one/two-line standing rule; (2) `hook`, or an equivalent mechanical setting, when enforcement is possible; (3) `skill`, only for a genuinely procedural or multi-step remedy; (4) `benchmark-only` when the failure is model-level and no instruction can fix it. Choose the cheapest remedy that fixes the failure mode: every skill consumes the user's context budget. `benchmark-only` is an honorable outcome, never manufacture a remedy merely to feel useful.

If the only sensible remedy target is Codex-side (`AGENTS.md` or `~/.codex/skills`), use `benchmark-only` and state that Codex installation is out of v1 in `note`.

The existing-remedy digests below are numbered [R1]…[RN]. There are 4 existing-remedy digests. Your `dedup` array MUST contain exactly 4 entries, one per number, with `existing` set to exactly that token (e.g. "R1"). Include entries even when the verdict is clear. State `clear` or `overlap` for each. Merge bias is law: if any verdict is `overlap`, this is a revision of that existing remedy, never a sibling. Set `overlap_action.revises` to that R token.

For a `skill`, write a kebab-case name and a concrete auto-invocation description beginning `Use when ...`; this description is the trigger. The body must be substantive Markdown. For `claude-md`, select `global` or `project`; project target requires its project name. For `hook`, give a Claude Code event and a command sketch. For `benchmark-only`, explain the measurement-only outcome in `note`.

The upstream classifier deliberately over-merges. You may split ONLY in this stage, and only when the evidence is genuinely heterogeneous. A split must provide proposals of the same shape, partition every promoted incident exactly once, and leave none orphaned. Otherwise return one proposal covering the group.

R2 (Fake Release Discipline) requires running a declared verification command before reporting a release complete — a post-hoc reporting-accuracy rule. These incidents are about mid-task constraint violations, unrelated to release verification.

R3 is a pending hook proposal gating destructive deletions with pre-execution confirmation. These incidents aren't about destructive deletions; they're about violating already-stated constraints (branch, network, protected files/scope) during otherwise normal edits.

structured_output.failure_statement: When the user states an explicit constraint mid-task (branch to use, no-network requirement, a file/component not to touch, scope boundaries like "don't touch tests"), the agent sometimes proceeds to violate that constraint or silently changes the plan without re-confirming, requiring the user to interrupt and re-state the constraint.

remedy_content.body:
# Honor Explicit Constraints

When the user states an explicit constraint during a task — a branch to work on, a no-network requirement, a file/component not to modify, a scope boundary (e.g. "don't touch tests") — treat it as binding for the rest of the task, not just the turn it was said in.

Before editing a file, running a command, or otherwise acting, check the action against every constraint the user has stated so far in the conversation. If a planned action would conflict with one, stop and flag the conflict to the user instead of proceeding, silently reinterpreting the plan, or assuming the constraint no longer applies. This includes constraints about which branch/environment to work in, not just file-level restrictions.
remedy_content.title: Honor explicit constraints stated in-session

structured_output.routing_rationale: The failure mode across all five incidents is the same: the agent had an explicit, previously-stated constraint from the user (no-network, work on a specific branch, don't touch the formatter, don't touch tests) and either deviated from it or silently reinterpreted the plan without flagging the conflict. This isn't heterogeneous — every case is "explicit constraint stated earlier in the conversation got dropped." A hook can't generalize here because the constraints are ad hoc and stated in natural language mid-conversation (branch names, "leave the formatter alone", "don't touch tests", "no network") — there's no fixed file pattern or tool-call signature a PreToolUse hook could match against. It's also not procedural/multi-step enough to warrant a skill; it's a single standing behavioral rule: track and honor explicit constraints stated in-session, and check actions against them before proceeding. That makes claude-md the cheapest correct remedy. Because R4 already appears to cover "acting in the wrong branch/environment" via a claude-md rule, and that is a subset of this same failure mode (explicit constraint disregarded), this proposal revises/broadens R4 rather than sitting beside it as a sibling.
